questions.question: What is abstraction in Java and how is it achieved?
questions.title: Abstraction in Java Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Abstraction** means hiding the complicated details and showing only what matters. In Java you achieve it with **abstract classes** (partial abstraction — a mix of abstract and concrete methods) and **interfaces** (100% abstraction — a pure contract). Callers depend on the *what* (the contract), not the *how* (the implementation).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand abstraction as a design idea (depend on contracts) and know the two Java mechanisms that deliver it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing abstraction (a principle) with the abstract keyword, or thinking abstraction is the same as encapsulation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie it to everyday code: declaring List<String> instead of ArrayList<String> is abstraction — you can swap the implementation without touching callers.

sections.title: Abstraction: Showing What, Hiding How
sections.content:
Abstraction means showing only what an object does and hiding how it does it. A caller sees a method like `area()` and calls it — they never see the formula inside.

**Why it exists**

A real program has thousands of moving parts. If every caller had to understand the internals of every class, no one could change anything safely. By exposing a small, clean surface and hiding the rest, you let callers depend on the *what* a thing does, not the *how*. Change the how later, and nothing that called the what breaks.

**How Java expresses it**

Java gives you two tools. An **abstract class** is partial abstraction: it declares some methods with no body (the holes a subclass must fill) and can also share concrete methods, fields, and constructors. An **interface** is full abstraction: a pure contract of method signatures that any class can implement, no matter what it already extends.

Reach for an abstract class when related subclasses share state and code — like an `Employee` base where each subtype calculates pay differently. Reach for an interface when unrelated classes need the same capability — like `Comparable` or `Serializable`.

**The nuance interviewers probe**

The line interviewers test is abstraction versus encapsulation. They sound similar but solve different problems: encapsulation hides *data* (private fields behind methods), while abstraction hides *implementation complexity* (the how behind a contract). One protects state; the other simplifies the surface.

> **Encapsulation hides *data*; abstraction hides *implementation complexity*.**

**The everyday payoff — and the gotcha**

The daily proof is one line: writing `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` instead of `ArrayList<String> names = ...`. The variable is typed to the contract, so you can swap in `LinkedList` tomorrow and no caller changes. And note abstraction is a design *principle*, not the `abstract` keyword — an interface delivers full abstraction without that keyword anywhere.

sections.title: Two Ways Java Achieves Abstraction
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["Abstraction
(Hide how, show what)"] --> AC["Abstract Class
partial abstraction"] A --> IF["Interface
100% contract"] AC --> AC1["Can have abstract methods
(no body — subclass fills in)"] AC --> AC2["Can have concrete methods
(shared logic — inherited as-is)"] AC --> AC3["Can hold instance fields
and constructors"] IF --> IF1["Only method signatures
(traditionally)"] IF --> IF2["Any class can implement
regardless of hierarchy"] IF --> IF3["Java 8+: default & static methods
for backward compatibility"] AC1 --> EX["Example: Shape → Circle, Rectangle
abstract area() implemented differently"] IF1 --> EX2["Example: List → ArrayList, LinkedList
same contract, different implementation"] ``` The key insight: callers depend on the contract (abstract class type or interface), not the concrete class behind it.

sections.title: Abstraction via Abstract Class and Interface
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating abstraction and encapsulation as the same thing** — they overlap in spirit but differ in target: encapsulation hides data behind methods, abstraction hides implementation behind a contract; conflating them gets you stuck the moment an interviewer asks for the difference.
- **Equating abstraction with the `abstract` keyword** — an interface delivers 100% abstraction without the keyword anywhere, so tying the principle to one keyword misses what it actually is.
- **Declaring the concrete type instead of the contract** — `ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>()` couples every caller to that class; swapping to `LinkedList` later forces edits that `List<String>` would have avoided.
- **Thinking abstraction just means "add an interface"** — wrapping a single implementation that will never change in an interface adds indirection for no payoff; abstraction earns its keep only when the how can genuinely vary.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstraction** = hide the *how*, expose the *what*. Real-world analogy: a TV remote hides the circuits.
- Java achieves it with **abstract classes** (partial: shared code + abstract holes) and **interfaces** (full: pure contract).
- It is a **design principle**, not just the `abstract` keyword — an interface delivers full abstraction without `abstract` on the class.
- **Program to the interface**: `List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()` lets you swap the implementation without touching callers.
- **Encapsulation vs Abstraction**: encapsulation hides *data*; abstraction hides *implementation complexity*. They are different principles.
- **Loose coupling**: callers depend on a contract, so implementations can change or be swapped (including mocks in tests) without breaking anything.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The way I think about it: a caller should only see **what** a class does, never **how** it pulls it off. That's **abstraction**, and it matters because you can change the how later without breaking anyone who depends on the what.

In Java you express it two ways. An **abstract class** is partial — it mixes body-less methods that subclasses must fill in with shared concrete code, fields, and constructors. An **interface** is the full version — a pure contract any class can implement, regardless of what it already extends. So:

- Reach for an `abstract class` when **related types share state**.
- Reach for an `interface` when **unrelated types share a capability**.

One distinction worth drawing: this isn't **encapsulation**. Encapsulation hides *data*; abstraction hides *complexity*. And it isn't the `abstract` keyword either — an `interface` is full abstraction without it. The everyday proof is typing `List` instead of `ArrayList`, so you can swap implementations and no caller changes. That **loose coupling** is the entire point.

questions.question: What is an abstract class in Java and what are its characteristics?
questions.title: Abstract Class in Java — Characteristics and Usage
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract class** is a class declared with the `abstract` keyword that **cannot be instantiated** — you must extend it. It can mix **abstract methods** (no body, subclasses must override) with **concrete methods**, hold **instance fields** and **constructors**, and carry any access modifier. Its purpose is to be a partially built base: shared code plus 'holes' that subclasses fill in.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the full feature set of an abstract class and how it differs from an interface.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an abstract class must have abstract methods, or that it can't have constructors/fields/concrete methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that abstract classes shine for shared state + partial implementation (template method pattern), and explicitly confirm you cannot instantiate an abstract class.

sections.title: Abstract Class: A Base You Must Extend
sections.content:
An abstract class is a class you cannot turn into an object on its own — you must extend it first. Write `new Shape()` where `Shape` is abstract and the compiler rejects it on the spot.

**Why it exists**

It exists to be a deliberately unfinished base. Some behavior is common to a whole family of types and some varies; an abstract class lets you write the common part once and leave the varying part as a hole for each subclass to fill. `Shape` can store a `color` and share `getColor()`, but it refuses to guess how `area()` is computed — that depends on the actual shape.

**What it can contain**

An abstract class is far more capable than freshers expect. It can hold:

- **abstract methods** — no body, every concrete subclass must implement them.
- **concrete methods** — full bodies inherited as-is, where shared logic lives.
- **instance fields** and **constructors** — the latter run via `super()` during subclass construction.
- static members.

The one thing it can't do is be instantiated directly. You can still use it as a reference type: `Shape s = new Circle()` is perfectly valid — the abstract type on the left, a concrete subclass on the right.

**The nuance interviewers push on**

An abstract class does **not** need a single abstract method. The `abstract` keyword on the class alone is enough to forbid `new`. The classic use is the Template Method pattern — a concrete method like `describe()` defines the fixed steps and calls an abstract `area()` for the step that varies.

**The gotcha — versus an interface**

An abstract class can carry mutable instance state and constructors; an interface cannot. So pick an abstract class when subclasses are related and share both data and partial behavior, and an interface when any unrelated class just needs to honor a contract.

> **Abstract class for shared state + partial behavior; interface for a pure contract.**

```mermaid flowchart TD S["abstract class Shape
─────────────────────
fields: color
concrete: getColor()
concrete: describe()
abstract: area() ← must override"] S --> C["class Circle extends Shape
─────────────────────────────
@Override
double area()
→ Math.PI × r × r"] S --> R["class Rectangle extends Shape
─────────────────────────────
@Override
double area()
→ width × height"] C --> OBJ1["Shape s = new Circle(...)
s.area() → Circle's formula"] R --> OBJ2["Shape s = new Rectangle(...)
s.area() → Rectangle's formula"] style S fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706 style C fill:#d1fae5,stroke:#059669 style R fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb ``` `Shape` cannot be instantiated — `new Shape()` is a compile error. Both `Circle` and `Rectangle` must implement `area()`. The caller only knows the `Shape` type.

sections.title: Abstract Class — Shape / Circle / Rectangle
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming an abstract class must have at least one abstract method** — it doesn't; the `abstract` keyword on the class alone forbids `new`, so a class with only concrete methods can still be abstract.
- **Believing abstract classes can't have constructors** — they can, and they run via `super()` to initialize shared fields before the subclass finishes building; assume otherwise and the shared-state model stops making sense.
- **Trying to instantiate it directly** — `new Shape()` is a compile error; you instantiate a concrete subclass and may hold it in an abstract reference like `Shape s = new Circle()`.
- **Reaching for an abstract class when an interface fits** — with no shared state or implementation to inherit, an abstract class burns the single-inheritance slot a subclass might need elsewhere; an interface keeps that slot free.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Declared with `abstract`; **cannot be instantiated** — `new Shape()` is a compile error even if it has no abstract methods.
- Use the abstract class as the **reference type**: `Shape s = new Circle(...)` is perfectly valid.
- Can mix **abstract methods** (no body — subclass must override) and **concrete methods** (full body — inherited as-is).
- Can hold **instance fields** and **constructors** (called via `super()` from subclasses) — unlike interfaces.
- Does **not require any abstract methods** — `abstract` on the class keyword alone is enough to forbid instantiation.
- Best for **shared state + partial implementation** (Template Method pattern); use an interface when unrelated classes need the same contract.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The headline characteristic is that you **can't instantiate it** — `new Shape()` on an abstract class is a straight compile error. You extend it and instantiate a concrete subclass instead, though you can still hold that subclass in an abstract reference like `Shape s = new Circle()`.

What makes it useful is everything it can contain:

- **abstract methods** the subclass must implement,
- **concrete methods** carrying shared logic,
- **instance fields**,
- and **constructors** that run through `super()`.

That mix is why it fits the **Template Method pattern** — a concrete method fixes the steps and calls an abstract one for the part that varies.

Two things people get wrong. It needs **no abstract method at all**; the keyword on the class alone blocks `new`. And it **can have constructors** — they fire during subclass construction. That's the real line against interfaces: an abstract class carries instance state and constructors, so I use it when **related subclasses share data and behavior**, and an interface when **unrelated classes only need a contract**.

questions.question: What are the rules for abstract methods in Java?
questions.title: Rules for Abstract Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract method** has a signature but **no body** (`abstract double area();`) and can only live inside an **abstract class** or an **interface**. Any first concrete subclass **must override and implement** every abstract method it inherits. Abstract methods **cannot** be `private`, `static`, or `final` — all three modifiers kill overriding, which defeats the entire purpose.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the exact legality rules for abstract methods, especially the modifier combinations that are illegal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an abstract method can be private/static/final, or that you can put an abstract method in a regular (non-abstract) class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the why: each forbidden modifier (private, static, final) defeats overriding, which is the whole point of an abstract method.

sections.title: Abstract Methods: Declared Here, Implemented Later
sections.content:
An abstract method is a method with a name, return type, and parameters but no body — it ends with a semicolon instead of curly braces, like `abstract double area();`. It says *what* should happen and leaves *how* to someone else.

**Why it exists**

It exists so a base type can demand a behavior without supplying it. The base knows every shape has an area but can't know the formula, so it declares the method abstract and forces each concrete subclass to provide its own version. Every rule about abstract methods flows from that single goal: they must stay overridable.

> **Any modifier that blocks overriding is incompatible with `abstract`.**

**Where it can live, and who must implement it**

First, location: an abstract method can only live inside an **abstract class** or an **interface**. Put one in a regular class and the compiler tells you to mark the class `abstract`. Second, the subclass contract: the first concrete subclass must override and implement every abstract method it inherits, or it must itself be declared `abstract`, passing the obligation down the chain.

**The nuance interviewers test — three illegal modifiers**

Three modifier combinations are illegal, and they all fail for one reason — **each kills overriding**:

- `private` hides the method from subclasses, so they can't override it.
- `static` belongs to the class and isn't polymorphically overridden, only hidden.
- `final` explicitly forbids overriding.

Since overriding is the entire purpose of an abstract method, all three are rejected.

**The gotcha — interface methods**

In an interface, methods are implicitly `public abstract`, so you never write those words. Java 8 added `default` and `static` interface methods (which have bodies), and Java 9 added `private` ones — but only the plain abstract methods still need implementing.

sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD AM["abstract method
return-type name(params);"] AM --> W["Where can it live?"] W --> W1["abstract class ✓"] W --> W2["interface ✓"] W --> W3["concrete class ✗ — compile error"] AM --> M["Which modifiers are illegal?"] M --> M1["private ✗
subclass can't see it → can't override"] M --> M2["static ✗
static methods aren't overridden"] M --> M3["final ✗
final explicitly forbids overriding"] AM --> SC["Subclass contract"] SC --> SC1["First concrete subclass must
implement ALL abstract methods"] SC --> SC2["If any missed →
subclass must also be abstract"] style M1 fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626 style M2 fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626 style M3 fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626 style W1 fill:#d1fae5,stroke:#059669 style W2 fill:#d1fae5,stroke:#059669 ```

sections.title: Legal vs Illegal Abstract Methods
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking `private abstract` is legal** — `private` hides the method from subclasses so it can never be overridden, and a method that can't be overridden defeats the whole point; the compiler rejects it.
- **Assuming `static abstract` works** — static methods belong to the class and are hidden, not polymorphically overridden, so the combination won't compile.
- **Marking an abstract method `final`** — `final` explicitly forbids overriding, the exact opposite of what `abstract` requires; the two keywords cancel each other out.
- **Putting an abstract method in a concrete class** — the class itself must be declared `abstract`, or the compiler errors; you can't sneak a body-less method into a regular class.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Abstract method = return type + name + params + `;` — **no body** (`{ }` makes it concrete).
- Can only live in an **abstract class** or an **interface** — illegal in a concrete class.
- The first **concrete subclass** must implement every inherited abstract method, or it must also be declared `abstract`.
- **Illegal modifiers**: `private` (can't be seen by subclass), `static` (not polymorphically overridden), `final` (forbids overriding). All three contradict the purpose of abstract.
- In an **interface**, methods are implicitly `public abstract` — no need to write those keywords.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An **abstract method** is just a signature with **no body** — it ends in a semicolon and forces whichever subclass extends the class to supply the real implementation. It can only live in an `abstract class` or an `interface`, never a regular concrete class.

The contract is simple: the **first concrete subclass** has to implement every abstract method it inherits, or it stays `abstract` itself and passes the job down the chain.

The part worth nailing is the three modifiers that never compile on it, and they all fail for **one root reason** — each kills overriding:

- `private` hides it from subclasses,
- `static` isn't polymorphically overridden,
- `final` outright forbids overriding.

Explaining that they share **one root cause**, rather than just reciting them, is what shows you understand the mechanism. And in an `interface`, methods are `public abstract` by default, so you skip both keywords.
